Turn 1 of 4 — read-back. Do not write any program JSON in this turn.

You are going to turn a recipe into a Rhylthyme program: parallel **tracks** of sequential **steps**, each with a duration and a start trigger, that one person follows against a live clock.

Plan this as a Rhylthyme recipe and deliver a live timeline: Backyard Barbecue: Smoker and Grill for a shoulder, sausages and sides for about twelve
Resource limits: one offset smoker, one kettle grill, one side burner, one cooler for holding, two cooks.
No finishing time was given; finish as early as the work allows.

Source text (read all of it):
<<<
Backyard Barbecue: Smoker and Grill

Two cooks, one offset smoker, one kettle grill, one side burner and a cooler for holding. The pork owns the smoker all day; everything else happens in the last two hours.

Pork shoulder
Light the smoker and bring it to 250°F; 45 minutes. While it comes up, trim the shoulder and rub it heavily with salt, pepper and paprika; 25 minutes. Put the shoulder on once the smoker holds temperature and smoke it unwrapped for 6 hours, until the bark is dark and set. Wrap it tightly in butcher paper; 10 minutes. Back on the smoker, wrapped, until the thickest part probes soft — usually another 3 hours, sometimes four. Hold it wrapped in a cooler for one to three hours; it will not get cold and it only gets better. Pull the meat by hand; 30 minutes.

Beans
When the pork goes into the cooler, fry the bacon and onion in the pot on the side burner for 12 minutes, then add the beans, molasses and a ladle of drippings and let them tick over on the lowest flame until you serve.

Slaw
Start the slaw at the same time. Shred the cabbage and carrot; 20 minutes. Whisk the buttermilk dressing; 8 minutes. Dress the slaw and put it in the refrigerator for at least 45 minutes so the cabbage softens.

Grill
Light the kettle an hour before you eat; 25 minutes to a clean bed of coals. Grill the sausages for 14 minutes. Grill the corn for 10 minutes. Toast the buns for 3 minutes, last, so they stay warm.

Table
Set out plates, pickles and sauce once the buns are off; 10 minutes. Call everyone over when both cooks say it is ready; 5 minutes to lay it all out.
>>>

Read all of it before you answer. Then say back, in one paragraph and in your own words: what is being made, for how many (or at what scale), by when, and under what constraints — equipment that exists only once, how many people are working, anything that has to be held, rested or ready at a particular moment. If the text you were given looks truncated, or points at a section that is not here, say so instead of filling the gap.

**Read-back**

Two cooks are putting on a backyard barbecue for about twelve people, built around one pork shoulder that owns the offset smoker all day: 45 minutes to light it and bring it to 250°F, 25 minutes of trimming and heavy salt/pepper/paprika rub while it comes up, 6 hours unwrapped until the bark is dark and set, 10 minutes to wrap in butcher paper, then another 3 hours (sometimes 4) wrapped until the thickest part probes soft, followed by a 1-to-3-hour rest wrapped in the cooler — it only gets better — and 30 minutes of pulling by hand. Everything else is squeezed into the last couple of hours and keyed off that rest: beans go on the side burner the moment the pork hits the cooler (12 minutes of bacon and onion in the pot, then a slow tick-over on the lowest flame until you serve), the slaw starts at that same moment (20 minutes shredding cabbage and carrot, 8 minutes whisking buttermilk dressing, then at least 45 minutes in the fridge to soften), and the kettle grill is lit an hour before eating (25 minutes to a clean bed of coals, then 14 minutes sausages, 10 minutes corn, and 3 minutes toasting buns last so they stay warm). The table follows the buns: 10 minutes to set out plates, pickles and sauce once the buns are off, then 5 minutes to call everyone over and lay it all out. No clock time and no "eat by" were given, so the plan anchors on the pork and finishes as early as the work allows; the hard constraints are that the offset smoker is occupied by the shoulder for essentially the whole cook, and the smoker, the kettle and the side burner each exist exactly once, the cooler is a single one-to-three-hour holding slot, and only two people are working all of it. The text reads complete — pork shoulder, beans, slaw, grill and table are all here and nothing points at a section that isn't — so the only thing it leaves to me is which cook takes which station (it never assigns them), and the variable 1–3-hour pork rest is the slack that lets the pulled pork land together with the last buns off the grill.

completion.text:
**The target data model, restated**

A **track** is one sequential line of work — one station, one dish, one cook's continuous thread — and because steps inside a track never overlap, anything that has to happen *while* something else is happening must live in a separate track (that's why the smoker's all-day pork and the last-two-hours slaw can't share a track, and it's fine for them to run side by side as two tracks). A **step** carries exactly one duration kind: `fixed` with `seconds`, `variable` with `minSeconds` / `maxSeconds` / `defaultSeconds` (the pork's wrapped phase, "usually another 3 hours, sometimes four", is exactly this), or `indefinite` with a `defaultSeconds` so previews still look sane, and durations may be written as numbers of seconds or as strings like `"6h"` or `"1h30m"`. A **startTrigger** is what ties a step to the clock or to another step: `programStart` at t=0, `programStartOffset` for a deliberate delay, `afterStep` for "when that finishes" (optionally with `event: "start"` or `offsetSeconds`), `afterStepWithBuffer` when there's a mandated wait, `manual` when a person taps to begin, `onAbort` for a failure path, and `compound` to wait on all or any of several triggers. `stepId`s are unique across the **whole** program, not per track, so I'll name them after the dish and the action rather than reusing `prep` in three tracks. Every `task` a step occupies needs a matching `resourceConstraints` entry, and its `maxConcurrent` is the thing that actually stops two steps from grabbing the one smoker, kettle, side burner or cooler at the same instant. Repeated work — n trays, n samples, n aircraft — goes on ONE step as `replicates: {count: n, mode: "serial" | "parallel" | "stagger"}`, never as hand-copied steps or tracks; per-instance continuations use `instances: "each"` on the following step, the step that waits for them all uses `instances: "all"`, and if the holding area between them only fits k at once, `replicates.maxInFlight: k` holds the *upstream* step back rather than stranding finished work downstream. (Here there's no genuine n-of-a-kind repetition — one shoulder, one batch of beans, one bowl of slaw — so `replicates` shouldn't appear at all; the three grill items are sequential on one kettle, not copies.)

**Resource constraints I expect, and why**

- `smoker` — **maxConcurrent 1**. One offset smoker, and the pork owns it from lighting through the wrapped phase. Two cooks can't change that.
- `grill` — **maxConcurrent 1**. One kettle; coals, sausages, corn and buns all queue on it.
- `sideBurner` — **maxConcurrent 1**. One burner, beans only, and it's occupied from the fry through the tick-over until serving.
- `cooler` — **maxConcurrent 1**. One cooler, one holding slot; the wrapped pork holds it for the whole 1–3 hour rest.
- `fridge` — **maxConcurrent 1**. The dressed slaw's ≥45-minute chill; one refrigerator (only one bowl of slaw, so this won't actually contend).
- `prep` — **maxConcurrent 2**. Bench/hands work: trim and rub, shredding, dressing, pulling, plating. Two cooks means two prep steps can overlap — that's the whole reason the early-morning rub and the late slaw can be worked at once.
- **actors: 2** — two cooks, which is also what caps how much of the above can be manned concurrently (pork pull, beans and grill all wanting a person in the last hour is the real crunch).

I'm deliberately *not* declaring a "cook" task, since `actors: 2` plus the machine constraints carry the two-person limit; and there'll be no `replicates` here, because nothing in this recipe is genuinely n-of-a-kind.

```json
{
  "acknowledgement": "tracks are sequential lines of work; one duration kind per step; triggers link steps; every task needs a resourceConstraint; stepIds are global",
  "resourceConstraints": [
    { "task": "smoker", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "grill", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "sideBurner", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "cooler", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "fridge", "maxConcurrent": 1 },
    { "task": "prep", "maxConcurrent": 2 }
  ],
  "actors": 2
}
```
